newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Pro-Euro Austria says will make EMU in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pro-Euro Austria says will make EMU in 1997.

text.p: Austria pinned its European flag to the mast on Tuesday by giving the clearest signal yet that the country will qualify for membership in Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1997.
In his first news conference of the year, Finance Minister Viktor Klima said the budget deficit would fall to 2.7 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from 3.7 percent last year.
The figure would come within the budget deficit to GDP ratio of three percent laid down in the Maastricht Treaty to qualify for the EMU club.
Klima said the federal budget deficit would fall to 68 billion schillings ($6.2 billion) this year from 89.4 billion schillings in 1996, or 3.7 percent of GDP, last year.

If his prediction comes true, Austria would be one of the foremost candidates for membership of EMU and Europe's planned single currency. Candidates are scheduled to be selected early in 1998 on the basis of 1997 economic performance. The EMU launch is planned for January 1999.
"Our aim for 1997 is to cut the budget deficit to 68 billion schillings. It seems possible," Klima told a news conference.
"1997 is going to be a very important year in order to meet the Maastricht criteria, and we will actually make it," he said. "It would be a catastrophe if Austria were not in EMU."
He predicted growth to be at least 1.2 percent this year, up from estimates last year of one percent -- in line with forecasts made by Austria's Wifo economic institute last month.
Austria looks odds-on to meet other Maastricht criteria with big strides made in achieving stability in exchange rates, inflation and interest rates.
The Austrian national bank already fulfills the Maastricht treaty rules governing the independence of central banks.

One lingering doubt remains over Austria's oustanding debt. A European Commission report last year forecast that Austrian debt would rise to 72.2 percent in 1997 from a projected 71.7 percent in 1996.

But Klima last year estimated that the debt ratio would be corrected in 1997 to show it "sufficiently diminishing" and approaching the required 60 percent of GDP. Such a move this year would be enough for Austria to make EMU.
Austria's two biggest politicial parties, the Social Democrats and conservative People's Party make up the governing coalition and both follow fervently pro-European policies.

Newcomer Austria, which joined the EU two years ago, has so far seen none of the social unrest experienced in some other EU states over spending cuts required by the drive for closer European economic integration.
But nearly 28 percent of voters backed the far right in European elections last October after leader Joerg Haider pledged to fight Maastricht to protect Austrian interests.
Klima said the government did have unexpected higher costs of three billion schillings to cover hospital reform and an extra five billion for family and pension payments.
But his estimate on the budget deficit reduction was based on lower interest payments on debt, higher revenue from taxes on cars and trucks and expected lower payments to the EU.

The government would also receive three billion schillings from its pension reserves for employees of the Postsparkasse bank, which is due to be privatised this year. The buyer would be required to take over the Postsparkasse pensions. ($1=10.90 Schilling)
